claim: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is characterized by sporadic collapse of the upper airway leading to periodic disruptions in breathing.
source: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is characterized by sporadic collapse of the upper airway leading to periodic disruptions in breathing.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about OSA that represents established medical knowledge.

claim: Upper airway patency is governed by genioglossal nerve activity that originates from the hypoglossal motor nucleus.
source: Upper airway patency is governed by genioglossal nerve activity that originates from the hypoglossal motor nucleus.
evidence: This statement reflects established anatomical and physiological knowledge about upper airway control.

claim: Mice with targeted deletion of the gene Hmox2, encoding the carbon monoxide (CO) producing enzyme, heme oxygenase-2 (HO-2), exhibit OSA.
source: Mice with targeted deletion of the gene Hmox2, encoding the carbon monoxide (CO) producing enzyme, heme oxygenase-2 (HO-2), exhibit OSA
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Peng et al., 2017) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Disrupting HO-2 activity increased the occurrence of subnetwork activity from the preBötC.
source: Disrupting HO-2 activity increased the occurrence of subnetwork activity from the preBötC, which was associated with an increased irregularity of rhythmogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2 showing subnetwork activity in ChrMP459 and HO-2 null conditions.

claim: Disrupting HO-2 activity was associated with an increased irregularity of rhythmogenesis.
source: Disrupting HO-2 activity increased the occurrence of subnetwork activity from the preBötC, which was associated with an increased irregularity of rhythmogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by IrSAMP measurements shown in Figures 1C and 2B-C.

claim: HO-2 dysregulation was associated with the intermittent inability of the preBötC rhythm to drive output from the hypoglossal nucleus (i.e. transmission failures).
source: These phenomena were also associated with the intermittent inability of the preBötC rhythm to drive output from the hypoglossal nucleus (i.e. transmission failures), and a reduction in the input-output relationship between the preBötC and the motor nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by transmission data in Figures 1E and 2E showing reduced transmission percentages.

claim: HO-2 dysregulation caused a reduction in the input-output relationship between the preBötC and the motor nucleus.
source: These phenomena were also associated with the intermittent inability of the preBötC rhythm to drive output from the hypoglossal nucleus (i.e. transmission failures), and a reduction in the input-output relationship between the preBötC and the motor nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by I/O ratio data shown in Figures 1D and 2D.

claim: HO-2 dysregulation reduced excitatory synaptic currents in inspiratory hypoglossal neurons.
source: HO-2 dysregulation reduced excitatory synaptic currents and intrinsic excitability in inspiratory hypoglossal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 4A demonstrating reduced drive currents.

claim: HO-2 dysregulation reduced intrinsic excitability in inspiratory hypoglossal neurons.
source: HO-2 dysregulation reduced excitatory synaptic currents and intrinsic excitability in inspiratory hypoglossal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by rheobase measurements shown in Figure 4C demonstrating increased rheobase.

claim: Inhibiting activity of the CO-regulated H2S producing enzyme, cystathionine-γ-lyase (CSE), reduced transmission failures in HO-2 null brainstem slices.
source: Inhibiting activity of the CO-regulated H2S producing enzyme, cystathionine-γ-lyase (CSE), reduced transmission failures in HO-2 null brainstem slices, which also normalized excitatory synaptic currents and intrinsic excitability of hypoglossal motoneurons.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 7 and 8 showing improved transmission with CSE inhibition.

claim: Inhibiting CSE activity normalized excitatory synaptic currents of hypoglossal motoneurons in HO-2 null conditions.
source: Inhibiting activity of the CO-regulated H2S producing enzyme, cystathionine-γ-lyase (CSE), reduced transmission failures in HO-2 null brainstem slices, which also normalized excitatory synaptic currents and intrinsic excitability of hypoglossal motoneurons.
evidence: This is supported by drive current measurements in Figure 8E showing increased currents with L-PAG treatment.

claim: Inhibiting CSE activity normalized intrinsic excitability of hypoglossal motoneurons in HO-2 null conditions.
source: Inhibiting activity of the CO-regulated H2S producing enzyme, cystathionine-γ-lyase (CSE), reduced transmission failures in HO-2 null brainstem slices, which also normalized excitatory synaptic currents and intrinsic excitability of hypoglossal motoneurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the normalization of synaptic drive and transmission shown in Figure 8.

claim: OSA affects nearly a billion people throughout the world.
source: Sporadic airway collapse is a hallmark of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a prevalent breathing disorder estimated to affect nearly a billion people throughout the world Lyons et al., 2020; Malhotra et al., 2021.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lyons et al., 2020 and Malhotra et al., 2021.

claim: When left untreated, OSA predisposes the individual to hypertension.
source: When left untreated, OSA predisposes the individual to a variety of diseases including hypertension Mehra, 2019; Yeghiazarians et al., 2021
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mehra, 2019 and Yeghiazarians et al., 2021.

claim: When left untreated, OSA predisposes the individual to diabetes.
source: When left untreated, OSA predisposes the individual to a variety of diseases including hypertension Mehra, 2019; Yeghiazarians et al., 2021, diabetes Loffler et al., 2020; Hua, 2020
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Loffler et al., 2020 and Hua, 2020.

claim: When left untreated, OSA predisposes the individual to cognitive decline.
source: When left untreated, OSA predisposes the individual to a variety of diseases including hypertension Mehra, 2019; Yeghiazarians et al., 2021, diabetes Loffler et al., 2020; Hua, 2020, and cognitive decline Daulatzai, 2017; Bibbins-Domingo et al., 2017.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Daulatzai, 2017 and Bibbins-Domingo et al., 2017.

claim: Multiple factors contribute to the genesis of OSA including compromised pharyngeal anatomy.
source: Multiple factors contribute to the genesis of OSA including compromised pharyngeal anatomy Castro and Freeman, 2021; Genta et al., 2017
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Castro and Freeman, 2021 and Genta et al., 2017.

claim: Multiple factors contribute to the genesis of OSA including inadequate upper airway muscle function.
source: Multiple factors contribute to the genesis of OSA including compromised pharyngeal anatomy Castro and Freeman, 2021; Genta et al., 2017, inadequate upper airway muscle function Neelapu et al., 2017; Vos et al., 2010; Kubin, 2016
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neelapu et al., 2017, Vos et al., 2010, and Kubin, 2016.

claim: Multiple factors contribute to the genesis of OSA including low arousal threshold.
source: Multiple factors contribute to the genesis of OSA including compromised pharyngeal anatomy Castro and Freeman, 2021; Genta et al., 2017, inadequate upper airway muscle function Neelapu et al., 2017; Vos et al., 2010; Kubin, 2016, low arousal threshold Eckert et al., 2013
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eckert et al., 2013.

claim: Multiple factors contribute to the genesis of OSA including a hypersensitive chemoreflex (i.e. high loop gain).
source: Multiple factors contribute to the genesis of OSA including compromised pharyngeal anatomy Castro and Freeman, 2021; Genta et al., 2017, inadequate upper airway muscle function Neelapu et al., 2017; Vos et al., 2010; Kubin, 2016, low arousal threshold Eckert et al., 2013, and a hypersensitive chemoreflex (i.e. high loop gain) Nemati et al., 2011.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nemati et al., 2011.

claim: OSA in HO-2 null mice was attributed, in part, to increased loop gain arising from the heightened carotid body chemoreflex.
source: OSA in HO-2 null mice was attributed, in part, to increased loop gain arising from the heightened carotid body chemoreflex Peng et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018; Osman et al., 2018; Prabhakar and Semenza, 2012.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2017, Peng et al., 2018, Osman et al., 2018, and Prabhakar and Semenza, 2012.

claim: The loss of HO-2 dependent carbon monoxide (CO) production was shown to be a primary driver of the enhanced carotid body chemoreflex and the subsequent OSA phenotype.
source: While HO-2 activity produces several bioactive molecules Mancuso, 2004, the loss of HO-2 dependent carbon monoxide (CO) production was shown to be a primary driver of the enhanced carotid body chemoreflex and the subsequent OSA phenotype Peng et al., 2017.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peng et al., 2017.

claim: Loss of neuromuscular control over upper airway muscles has a key role in producing obstructive apneas.
source: Loss of neuromuscular control over upper airway muscles has a key role in producing obstructive apneas Schwartz et al., 2008; Horner, 2001.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schwartz et al., 2008 and Horner, 2001.

claim: Disrupting neuronal excitability in the hypoglossal nucleus that is responsible for genioglossal nerve activity increases the likelihood for the tongue to occlude the upper airway during inspiration.
source: Disrupting neuronal excitability in the hypoglossal nucleus that is responsible for genioglossal nerve activity increases the likelihood for the tongue to occlude the upper airway during inspiration.
evidence: This represents established physiological knowledge about upper airway control.

claim: Disruptions in hypoglossal excitability may involve changing the state-dependent balance between excitation and inhibition received by hypoglossal motoneurons.
source: Such disruptions may involve changing the state-dependent balance between excitation and inhibition received by hypoglossal motoneurons Horner, 2009
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Horner, 2009.

claim: Disruptions in hypoglossal excitability may involve directly modulating intrinsic excitability of hypoglossal motoneurons.
source: Such disruptions may involve changing the state-dependent balance between excitation and inhibition received by hypoglossal motoneurons Horner, 2009 and/or by directly modulating their intrinsic excitability Horton et al., 2017; Fleury Curado et al., 2017; Fleury Curado et al., 2018.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horton et al., 2017, Fleury Curado et al., 2017, and Fleury Curado et al., 2018.

claim: Hypoglossal neurons express heme oxygenase-2 (HO-2).
source: Hypoglossal neurons showed positive immunohistochemical expression for HO-2 as indicated by co-localization of HO-2 with ChAT, a motoneuron marker (Figure 1A, n=3).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating co-localization of HO-2 with ChAT.

claim: ChrMP459 promoted the emergence of subnetwork activity in the preBötC.
source: ChrMP459 promoted the emergence of subnetwork activity (i.e., integrated bursts ≤ 50% of mean integrated burst amplitude during baseline; demarcated by hash symbol, Figure 1B) in the preBötC.
evidence: This is supported by recordings shown in Figure 1B demonstrating subnetwork bursts marked with hash symbols.

claim: Subnetwork preBötC activity commonly failed to drive corresponding output from the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: This subnetwork preBötC activity commonly failed to drive corresponding output hypoglossal nucleus (highlighted in pink, Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by simultaneous recordings shown in Figure 1B with failed transmissions highlighted in pink.

claim: ChrMP459 increased the irregularity score of amplitude (IrSAMP) in the preBötC.
source: This subnetwork preBötC activity commonly failed to drive corresponding output hypoglossal nucleus (highlighted in pink, Figure 1B) and was associated with an increase in the irregularity score of amplitude (IrSAMP) in the preBötC (Figure 1C, bottom; Baseline: 0.279±0.39, ChrMP459: 0.406±0.05, p=0.021).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative IrSAMP data shown in Figure 1C with statistical comparison.

claim: ChrMP459 did not impact the IrSAMP in hypoglossal nucleus.
source: However, ChrMP459 did not impact the IrSAMP in hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 1C, top; Baseline: 0.385±0.05, ChrMP459: 0.372±0.03, p=0.701)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative IrSAMP data shown in Figure 1C with statistical comparison showing no significant difference.

claim: ChrMP459 did not affect the frequency of integrated bursts from the preBötC.
source: However, ChrMP459 did not impact the IrSAMP in hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 1C, top; Baseline: 0.385±0.05, ChrMP459: 0.372±0.03, p=0.701) nor affect the frequency or amplitude of the integrated bursts from either brainstem network (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by frequency data in Table 1 showing no significant difference in preBötC frequency.

claim: ChrMP459 did not affect the amplitude of integrated bursts from the preBötC.
source: However, ChrMP459 did not impact the IrSAMP in hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 1C, top; Baseline: 0.385±0.05, ChrMP459: 0.372±0.03, p=0.701) nor affect the frequency or amplitude of the integrated bursts from either brainstem network (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by amplitude data in Table 1 showing no significant difference in preBötC burst amplitude.

claim: ChrMP459 did not affect the frequency of integrated bursts from the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: However, ChrMP459 did not impact the IrSAMP in hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 1C, top; Baseline: 0.385±0.05, ChrMP459: 0.372±0.03, p=0.701) nor affect the frequency or amplitude of the integrated bursts from either brainstem network (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by frequency data in Table 1 for XIIn.

claim: ChrMP459 did not affect the amplitude of integrated bursts from the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: However, ChrMP459 did not impact the IrSAMP in hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 1C, top; Baseline: 0.385±0.05, ChrMP459: 0.372±0.03, p=0.701) nor affect the frequency or amplitude of the integrated bursts from either brainstem network (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by amplitude data in Table 1 for XIIn showing no significant difference.

claim: ChrMP459 caused a consistent reduction in the cycle-to-cycle input-output relationship between preBötC and the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: ChrMP459 caused a consistent reduction in the cycle-to-cycle input-output relationship between preBötC and the hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 1D) which was quantified by comparing input-output (I/O) ratios prior to and during ChrMP459 (Baseline: 1.06±0.04 vs. ChrMP459: 0.592±0.06; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by I/O ratio data shown in Figure 1D with statistical comparison.

claim: The reduced I/O ratio in ChrMP459 was associated with increased transmission failure.
source: The reduced I/O ratio in ChrMP459 was, indeed, associated with increased transmission failure (Figure 1E, Baseline: 94.130±1.27% vs. ChrMP459: 75.100 ± 3.43%, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by transmission data shown in Figure 1E with statistical comparison.

claim: While many transmission failures were associated with subnetwork preBötC activity, these events were not restricted to subnetwork activity but rather occurred across a range of integrated burst areas from the inspiratory network.
source: Examining the relationship between failed transmission and the burst area in the preBötC revealed that while the many transmission failures were associated with subnetwork preBötC activity (i.e. integrated burst areas ≤ 50%), these events were not restricted to subnetwork activity but rather, occurred across a range of integrated burst areas from the inspiratory network (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the distribution analysis shown in Figure 1F demonstrating transmission failures across different burst areas.

claim: Both the intermittent occurrence of subnetwork activity in the preBötC and failed transmission events were observed in HO-2 null slices.
source: Both the intermittent occurrence of subnetwork activity in the preBötC (demarcated by hash symbol, Figure 2A) and failed transmission events were observed in HO-2 null slices (highlighted in pink, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by recordings shown in Figure 2A demonstrating both phenomena in HO-2 null slices.

claim: preBötC activity in HO-2 null mice was associated with an increased IrSAMP in the preBötC.
source: preBötC activity in HO-2 null mice was associated with an increased IrSAMP in both the preBötC (Figure 2B, WT: 0.323±0.02, HO-2 null: 0.419±0.03, p+0.014)
evidence: This is supported by IrSAMP comparison data shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: preBötC activity in HO-2 null mice was associated with an increased IrSAMP in the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: preBötC activity in HO-2 null mice was associated with an increased IrSAMP in both the preBötC (Figure 2B, WT: 0.323±0.02, HO-2 null: 0.419±0.03, p+0.014) and the hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 2C, WT: 0.269±0.03, HO-2 null: 0.534±0.12, p=0.018).
evidence: This is supported by IrSAMP comparison data shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: The frequency was faster in HO-2 null rhythms relative to wild-type rhythms.
source: While the frequency was faster in HO-2 null rhythms relative to wild-type rhythms, the burst amplitude was not different in either preBötC or the hypoglossal (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by frequency data in Table 1 comparing WT and HO-2 null slices.

claim: The burst amplitude was not different between HO-2 null and wild-type rhythms in either preBötC or the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: While the frequency was faster in HO-2 null rhythms relative to wild-type rhythms, the burst amplitude was not different in either preBötC or the hypoglossal (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by burst amplitude data in Table 1 showing no significant differences.

claim: Relative to wild-type slices, the HO-2 null preparations had smaller cycle-to-cycle I/O ratios.
source: Relative to wild-type slices, the HO-2 null preparations had smaller cycle-to-cycle I/O ratios (Figure 2D; wild-type: 1.023±0.03 vs. HO-2 null: 0.799±0.07, p=0.002)
evidence: This is supported by I/O ratio comparison data shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: HO-2 null slices had a smaller percentage of transmission compared to wild-type slices.
source: Relative to wild-type slices, the HO-2 null preparations had smaller cycle-to-cycle I/O ratios (Figure 2D; wild-type: 1.023±0.03 vs. HO-2 null: 0.799±0.07, p=0.002); this was accompanied by a smaller percentage of transmission in HO-2 null slices (Figure 2E, wild-type: 98.210±0.87% vs. HO-2 null: 64.110 ± 6.00%, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by transmission comparison data shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis.

claim: In HO-2 null slices, failed transmission occurred across a range of burst areas from the preBötC.
source: Similar to ChrMP459 experiments, while subnetwork activity led to many failed transmission events, failed transmission occurred across a range of burst areas from the preBötC (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the distribution analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Lost HO-2 activity is sufficient for promoting subnetwork preBötC activity.
source: These findings were consistent with ChrMP459 findings and illustrated that lost HO-2 activity is sufficient for promoting subnetwork preBötC activity, reducing input-output relationship between preBötC and the hypoglossal nucleus, and increasing transmission failures.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of ChrMP459 and HO-2 null data showing similar effects.

claim: Lost HO-2 activity is sufficient for reducing input-output relationship between preBötC and the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: These findings were consistent with ChrMP459 findings and illustrated that lost HO-2 activity is sufficient for promoting subnetwork preBötC activity, reducing input-output relationship between preBötC and the hypoglossal nucleus, and increasing transmission failures.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of ChrMP459 and HO-2 null data showing similar effects.

claim: Lost HO-2 activity is sufficient for increasing transmission failures.
source: These findings were consistent with ChrMP459 findings and illustrated that lost HO-2 activity is sufficient for promoting subnetwork preBötC activity, reducing input-output relationship between preBötC and the hypoglossal nucleus, and increasing transmission failures.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of ChrMP459 and HO-2 null data showing similar effects.

claim: Intermediate premotor neurons relay drive from the preBötC to the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: Intermediate premotor neurons relay drive from the preBötC to the hypoglossal nucleus Koizumi et al., 2013; Revill et al., 2015.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koizumi et al., 2013 and Revill et al., 2015.

claim: During failed cycles, preBötC activity still produced detectable network activity in the field of intermediary premotor neurons.
source: In ChrMP459, intermittent failures of hypoglossal nucleus activity corresponding preBötC activity were evident yet during these failed cycles preBötC activity still produced detectable network activity in the field of intermediary premotor neurons (Figure 3A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by triple recording data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating premotor activity during failed hypoglossal transmission.

claim: Neither the cycle-to-cycle I/O ratio nor transmission from the preBötC to the premotor field was affected by ChrMP459.
source: Indeed, while neither the cycle-to-cycle I/O ratio nor transmission from the preBötC to the premotor field was affected by ChrMP459 (Figure 3B: left; I/O ratio: Baseline: 1.116±0.09 vs ChrMP 1.162±0.15, p=0.816; right; Transmission: Baseline: 100.0±0.0% vs ChrMP 86.350 ± 11.81%, p=0.312)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B with statistical comparisons showing no significant differences.

claim: ChrMP459 reduced the cycle-to-cycle I/O ratio between the premotor field and the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: the HO inhibitor reduced the cycle-to-cycle I/O ratio and the transmission between the premotor field and the hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 3C: left, I/O: Baseline: 1.102±0.18 vs ChrMP 0.401±0.09, p=0.041; right, Transmission: Baseline 89.570±4.34% vs ChrMP 57.620 ± 13.69%, p=0.041).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: ChrMP459 reduced transmission between the premotor field and the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: the HO inhibitor reduced the cycle-to-cycle I/O ratio and the transmission between the premotor field and the hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 3C: left, I/O: Baseline: 1.102±0.18 vs ChrMP 0.401±0.09, p=0.041; right, Transmission: Baseline 89.570±4.34% vs ChrMP 57.620 ± 13.69%, p=0.041).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: ChrMP459 potentially affected synaptic properties to the hypoglossal motoneurons and/or the intrinsic excitability of hypoglossal neurons.
source: Thus, these findings suggested that ChrMP459 potentially affected synaptic properties to the hypoglossal motoneurons and/or the intrinsic excitability of hypoglossal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the triple recording experiments showing intact premotor activity but failed hypoglossal transmission.

claim: Peak inspiratory drive currents were reduced in ChrMP459.
source: Peak inspiratory drive currents were reduced in ChrMP459 (Figure 4A, n=19, Baseline: –142.90±22.82 pA vs. ChrMP459: –95.31±21.79 pA, p=0.004).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 4A with statistical comparison.

claim: Reduced drive coincided with hypoglossal neurons generating fewer action potentials per preBötC burst in ChrMP459.
source: Reduced drive coincided with hypoglossal neurons generating fewer action potentials per preBötC burst in ChrMP459 (Figure 4B, n=17, Baseline: 14.68±2.24 action potentials per burst vs. ChrMP459: 6.798±1.55 action potentials per burst, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by current clamp recordings shown in Figure 4B with statistical comparison.

claim: The HO inhibitor increased rheobase among inspiratory hypoglossal neurons.
source: Injection of a depolarizing ramp current into hypoglossal neurons revealed that the HO inhibitor increased rheobase among inspiratory hypoglossal neurons (Figure 4C, n=19, Baseline: 167.5±35.85 pA vs. ChrMP459: 338.0±82.50 pA, p=0.007)
evidence: This is supported by ramp current injection data shown in Figure 4C with statistical comparison.

claim: The HO inhibitor decreased rheobase in non-inspiratory hypoglossal neurons.
source: Injection of a depolarizing ramp current into hypoglossal neurons revealed that the HO inhibitor increased rheobase among inspiratory hypoglossal neurons (Figure 4C, n=19, Baseline: 167.5±35.85 pA vs. ChrMP459: 338.0±82.50 pA, p=0.007) yet decreased rheobase in non-inspiratory hypoglossal neurons (i.e. neurons not receiving drive during preBötC activity; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, n=8, Baseline: 280.5±56.43 pA vs. ChrMP459: 228.2±47.96 pA, p=0.0117).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical comparison.

claim: The percentage of subnetwork preBötC activity was greater in ChrMP459 when synaptic inhibition was preserved compared to disinhibited ChrMP459.
source: Indeed, the percentage of subnetwork preBötC activity was greater in ChrMP459 when synaptic inhibition was preserved (Figure 5B, ChrMP459, n=34: 19.43±3.37% vs disinhibited ChrMP459, n=17: 6.72 ± 3.13%, p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: The IrSAMP during ChrMP459 was smaller in the disinhibited preBötC rhythm.
source: Similarly, the IrSAMP during ChrMP459 was smaller in the disinhibited preBötC rhythm (Figure 5C, ChrMP459: 0.406±0.051 vs disinhibited ChrMP459: 0.215±0.04, p=0.019).
evidence: This is supported by IrSAMP comparison data shown in Figure 5C with statistical analysis.

claim: HO-2 is a negative regulator of CSE-dependent H2S production.
source: We next sought to determine the mechanism(s) by which inhibition of HO-2 affected hypoglossal neuron activity. Earlier studies Prabhakar, 2012; Morikawa et al., 2012 have reported that HO-2 is a negative regulator of CSE-dependent H2S production.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Prabhakar, 2012 and Morikawa et al., 2012.

claim: CSE is expressed in ChAT-positive hypoglossal neurons.
source: In the wild-type hypoglossal nucleus, CSE is expressed in ChAT-positive hypoglossal neurons (Figure 6A, n=3 mice).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A demonstrating co-localization.

claim: H2S abundance was greater in the hypoglossal nucleus of HO-2 null mice relative to wild-type.
source: Relative to the wild-type hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 6B blue; n=6, 60.58±6.37 nmol • mg–1 • h–1), H2S abundance was greater in the hypoglossal nucleus of HO-2 null mice (Figure 6B red; n=6, 144.12±8.29 nmol • mg–1 • h–1, p<0.001)
evidence: This is supported by H2S measurement data shown in Figure 6B with statistical comparison.

claim: H2S abundance in the inferior olive brainstem region of HO-2 null mice was not different from wild-type hypoglossal nucleus.
source: Relative to the wild-type hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 6B blue; n=6, 60.58±6.37 nmol • mg–1 • h–1), H2S abundance was greater in the hypoglossal nucleus of HO-2 null mice (Figure 6B red; n=6, 144.12±8.29 nmol • mg–1 • h–1, p<0.001), but not different from the inferior olive brainstem region of HO-2 null mice (Figure 6B gray; n=4, 56.10±2.88 nmol • mg–1 • h–1, p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by H2S measurement data shown in Figure 6B with statistical comparison.

claim: The hypoglossal nucleus expresses CSE.
source: These findings show that the hypoglossal nucleus expresses CSE and suggests that HO-2 negatively regulates H2S production in the hypoglossal nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HO-2 negatively regulates H2S production in the hypoglossal nucleus.
source: These findings show that the hypoglossal nucleus expresses CSE and suggests that HO-2 negatively regulates H2S production in the hypoglossal nucleus.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased H2S levels in HO-2 null hypoglossal nucleus shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NaHS application reduced transmission from preBötC to hypoglossal output in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Application of NaHS, a H2S donor reduced this transmission from preBötC to hypoglossal output (Figure 6C, middle, right) in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6D; 0 μM NaHS: n=9, 100.0 ± 0.77%; 10 μM NaHS: n=5, 90.14 ± 6.78%; 50 μM NaHS: n=6, 84.18 ± 4.29%; 100 μM NaHS: n=6, 81.26 ± 6.19%)
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: NaHS reduced the I/O ratio in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Application of NaHS, a H2S donor reduced this transmission from preBötC to hypoglossal output (Figure 6C, middle, right) in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6D; 0 μM NaHS: n=9, 100.0 ± 0.77%; 10 μM NaHS: n=5, 90.14 ± 6.78%; 50 μM NaHS: n=6, 84.18 ± 4.29%; 100 μM NaHS: n=6, 81.26 ± 6.19%), which coincided with a reduction in I/O ratio by NaHS (Figure 6E; 0 μM NaHS: 1.055±0.03; 10 μM NaHS: 0.850±0.10; 50 μM NaHS: 0.816±0.09; 100 μM NaHS: 0.843±0.07).
evidence: This is supported by I/O ratio data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Increasing H2S abundance reduces hypoglossal neuronal activity consistent with findings from experiments using ChrM459 or HO-2 null mice.
source: These findings demonstrated that increasing H2S abundance reduces hypoglossal neuronal activity consistent with findings from experiments using ChrM459 or HO-2 null mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the NaHS experiments mimicking the effects of HO-2 dysregulation.

claim: HO-2 dependent CO is known to inhibit CSE-dependent H2S production.
source: HO-2 dependent CO is known to inhibit CSE-dependent H2S production Prabhakar, 2012; Morikawa et al., 2012.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Prabhakar, 2012 and Morikawa et al., 2012.

claim: CORM-3 improved I/O ratios in dysregulated HO-2 activity conditions.
source: Dysregulated HO-2 activity, caused by either pharmacological (ChrMP459) or genetic (HO-2 null mice) manipulation, is improved by CORM-3 as indicated by augmented I/O ratios (Figure 7B, n=8; dysregulated HO-2: 0.705±0.09 vs. CORM-3: 1.05±0.07, p=0.01)
evidence: This is supported by I/O ratio comparison data shown in Figure 7B with statistical analysis.

claim: CORM-3 improved transmission in dysregulated HO-2 activity conditions.
source: Dysregulated HO-2 activity, caused by either pharmacological (ChrMP459) or genetic (HO-2 null mice) manipulation, is improved by CORM-3 as indicated by augmented I/O ratios (Figure 7B, n=8; dysregulated HO-2: 0.705±0.09 vs. CORM-3: 1.05±0.07, p=0.01) and improved transmission (Figure 7C, dysregulated HO-2: 75.05±6.30% vs. CORM-3: 94.21 ± 2.67%, p=0.020).
evidence: This is supported by transmission comparison data shown in Figure 7C with statistical analysis.

claim: HO-2:CSE double null mice had a larger I/O ratio compared to HO-2 null slices.
source: Quantification of simultaneous extracellular field recordings of preBötC activity and hypoglossal nucleus revealed a larger I/O ratio (Figure 7E, HO-2:CSE: 1.014±0.02, n=6, p=0.003)
evidence: This is supported by I/O ratio comparison data shown in Figure 7E with statistical analysis.

claim: HO-2:CSE double null mice showed near absence of transmission failures compared to HO-2 null slices.
source: Quantification of simultaneous extracellular field recordings of preBötC activity and hypoglossal nucleus revealed a larger I/O ratio (Figure 7E, HO-2:CSE: 1.014±0.02, n=6, p=0.003) and near absence of transmission failures (Figure 7F, HO-2:CSE: 91.57 ± 3.20%, p=0.0007) when compared to activity in HO-2 null slices.
evidence: This is supported by transmission comparison data shown in Figure 7F with statistical analysis.

claim: In vivo L-PAG treatment in HO-2 null mice improved transmission of preBötC activity to the hypoglossal nucleus in the rhythmic slice.
source: Similarly, in vivo L-PAG treatment, to acutely inhibit CSE activity, in HO-2 null mice improved transmission of preBötC activity to the hypoglossal nucleus in the rhythmic slice (Figure 8A, n=6) as indicated by larger cycle-to-cycle I/O ratio (Figure 8B and L -PAG = 1.01± 0.03, p=0.008) and greater transmission rates (Figure 8C and L -PAG 95.92 ± 2.18%, p<0.0001) when compared to the respective metrics from untreated HO-2 null mice.
evidence: This is supported by I/O ratio and transmission data shown in Figures 8B and 8C with statistical comparisons.

claim: L-PAG treatment resulted in larger individual inspiratory drive currents in HO-2 null hypoglossal neurons compared to untreated HO-2 null neurons.
source: These reduced transmission events correlated with smaller individual inspiratory drive currents in HO-2 null hypoglossal neurons when compared to corresponding inspiratory synaptic drive currents from L-PAG-treated HO-2 mice (Figure 8D–E, HO-2: –36.71±2.14 pA vs. L-PAG –194.3±82.73 pA, p=0.0007).
evidence: This is supported by drive current comparison data shown in Figures 8D-E with statistical analysis.

claim: CSE-dependent H2S signaling is involved with the effects of disrupted HO-2/CO signaling affecting synaptic drive and output from hypoglossal motoneurons.
source: Together, these experiments implicated the involvement of CSE-dependent H2S signaling with the effects of disrupted HO-2 /CO signaling affecting synaptic drive and output from hypoglossal motoneurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective results of CORM-3, HO-2:CSE null, and L-PAG experiments.

claim: H2S can enhance both KATP and SKCa activities.
source: H2S can enhance both KATP and SKCa activities Mustafa et al., 2011.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haller et al., 2001.

claim: Tolbutamide improved the I/O ratio in ChrMP459 conditions.

claim: Tolbutamide did not reduce transmission failure in ChrMP459 conditions.
source: In ChrMP459, tolbutamide had a limited effect normalizing transmission as it improved the I/O ratio, but did not reduce transmission failure.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C showing no significant change in transmission.

claim: Tolbutamide neither increased excitatory synaptic currents nor enhanced intrinsic excitability of hypoglossal neurons in ChrMP459.
source: Tolbutamide neither increased excitatory synaptic currents nor enhanced intrinsic excitability of hypoglossal neurons in ChrMP459.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D-F showing no significant effects.

claim: Apamin normalized synaptic drive currents in ChrMP459.

claim: Blockade of KATP was limited in countering the effects on HO-2 dysregulation in the hypoglossal nucleus.

claim: Blockade of SKCa sufficiently mitigates many aspects of HO-2 dysregulation in hypoglossal neurons associated with preBötC activity.

evidence: This is inferred from the effectiveness of apamin shown in Figure 9.

claim: Spontaneous hypertensive rats exhibit an increased incidence of apneas and hypopneas that are associated with reduced CO levels due to a reduction in HO-2 activity and increased H2S generation.
source: In addition, the occurrence of obstructive apnea in HO-2 null mice Peng et al., 2017, spontaneous hypertensive rats exhibit an increased incidence of apneas and hypopneas that are associated with reduced CO levels due to a reduction in HO-2 activity and increased H2S generation Peng et al., 2014.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peng et al., 2014.

claim: Central HO-2 dysregulation may contribute to the incidence of apneas.
source: While in both cases, these effects have been linked to interactions between CO and H2S in the peripheral nervous system, our findings indicate that central HO-2 dysregulation may also contribute to the incidence of apneas.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing central effects of HO-2 dysregulation on hypoglossal activity.

claim: Loss of HO-2 activity causes irregular rhythmogenesis from the preBötC.
source: Loss of HO-2 activity causes irregular rhythmogenesis from the preBötC while also reducing synaptic drive and intrinsic excitability in hypoglossal motoneurons.

claim: Loss of HO-2 activity reduces synaptic drive in hypoglossal motoneurons.

claim: Loss of HO-2 activity reduces intrinsic excitability in hypoglossal motoneurons.
source: Loss of HO-2 activity causes irregular rhythmogenesis from the preBötC while also reducing synaptic drive and intrinsic excitability in hypoglossal motoneurons.

claim: The interaction between HO-2 dependent CO production and CSE-dependent H2S activity have an important role in regulating hypoglossal activity.

claim: Increased chemoreflex sensitivity in HO-2 null mice has been attributed to increased chemo reflex sensitivity regulated by the carotid bodies.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2017, Peng et al., 2018, Osman et al., 2018, and Prabhakar and Semenza, 2012.
